lead: A projectile is a particle thrown into the air and then left to gravity. Its horizontal and vertical motions do not interfere. Horizontally the velocity stays constant, because no horizontal force acts. Vertically the particle has the constant acceleration g = 9.81 m/s² downward. Two straight-line problems run at once. This is how you find where a cricket ball lands and where a package dropped from a drone hits the ground. Air resistance is ignored throughout.
prereq: You need 5.1 for constant-acceleration formulas and 5.2 for resolving velocity into components.

blocks.text: Let u be launch speed in m/s and θ the angle above the horizontal. Take x horizontal and y upward from the launch point. Air resistance is ignored, so the only force is weight mg downward.
x = (u cosθ) t,   v<sub>x</sub> = u cosθ
blocks.where: x is horizontal displacement in m at time t in s; u is launch speed in m/s; θ is launch angle; v<sub>x</sub> is constant horizontal velocity in m/s.

blocks.text: y = (u sinθ) t − ½ g t²,   v<sub>y</sub> = u sinθ − g t
blocks.where: y is vertical displacement in m; g = 9.81 m/s²; v<sub>y</sub> is vertical velocity in m/s at time t.

blocks.text: Horizontal motion is uniform. Vertical motion is constant acceleration from 5.1. At the top vy = 0.

The equations share t. A ball kicked at 20 m/s at 30° keeps v<sub>x</sub> = 17.3 m/s, while v<sub>y</sub> starts at 10 m/s and loses 9.81 m/s each second. The path bends only because v<sub>y</sub> changes; v<sub>x</sub> does not.
The trajectory is y as a function of x. From x = (u cosθ)t, t = x/(u cosθ).

items: Replace sinθ/cosθ by tanθ and 1/cos²θ by sec²θ.

blocks.text: y = x tanθ − g x² / (2u² cos²θ)
blocks.where: y is height in m at horizontal distance x in m; θ is launch angle; u is launch speed in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: This is a quadratic in x, so the path is a parabola opening downward. The apex is at x = u² sin2θ/(2g), where v<sub>y</sub> = 0.
The figure plots it for u = 20 m/s and θ = 30°.
Doubling u makes a wider, higher parabola. Rise and fall are mirror images on level ground.
The curve crosses y = 0 at launch and at the range R. It is steepest at those points and flat at the apex. The same parabola describes a fountain jet and a thrown stone.
Level ground means launch and landing at the same height. Set y = 0 and solve.

blocks.where: T is time of flight in s; the factor 2 is for the up and down halves.
R is horizontal range in m on level ground; sin2θ = 2 sinθ cosθ.
H is maximum height in m above launch.

blocks.text: R is largest at θ = 45°, where sin2θ = 1 and R = u²/g. Angles 30° and 60° give the same range.
Horizontal projection from height h: initial v<sub>y</sub> = 0, so h = ½gt², t = √(2h/g), range = u√(2h/g).
Use level-ground formulas only when heights match; otherwise solve the quadratic.

figure.caption: The parabola for a 20 m/s kick at 30°. The orange point is the apex at 5.10 m, halfway along the 35.3 m range.

spec.aria: Parabolic path of a ball launched at 20 m/s and 30 degrees, peaking at 5.10 m halfway along and landing 35.3 m away.

examples.question: A ball is kicked from level ground at u = 20 m/s at θ = 30° to the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the time of flight, the maximum height and the horizontal range.
examples.answer: Time of flight 2.04 s, maximum height 5.10 m, horizontal range 35.31 m.
examples.check:
import math
u = 20.0
theta = math.radians(30)
g = 9.81
T = 2 * u * math.sin(theta) / g
H = (u * math.sin(theta))**2 / (2 * g)
R = u**2 * math.sin(2 * theta) / g
print(round(T, 2))
print(round(H, 2))
print(round(R, 2))

traps: Swapping components: cosθ goes with x, sinθ with y.
Using the range formula when landing height differs from launch height.
Taking g as 10 m/s² when the paper says 9.81.
Assuming v<sub>y</sub> = 0 at landing; on level ground it is −u sinθ.
Using degrees in a calculator set to radians.

quiz.a: Motion under gravity alone after launch, with horizontal velocity constant and vertical acceleration g downward.
No horizontal force acts, so a<sub>x</sub> = 0.

quiz.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from 20 m. Find the landing time and range (g = 9.81).
Find the maximum level-ground range for u = 30 m/s.
Two balls launch at 30° and 60° with equal speed. Compare range, height and flight time.
quiz.a: Ranges equal because sin60° = sin120°; the 60° ball has greater height and longer flight.

quiz.q: At the apex, what are v<sub>x</sub>, v<sub>y</sub> and acceleration?
quiz.a: v<sub>x</sub> = u cosθ, v<sub>y</sub> = 0, acceleration = 9.81 m/s² downward.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real projectiles feel air drag proportional to speed squared, which shortens the range and makes the descent steeper than the rise. Sports engineers fit drag coefficients to ball trajectories; meteorologists solve the same equations for falling rain. Search "projectile with air resistance" and "ballistic coefficient" to go further.
